logline: The last days of Christmas break and the first day back: a long cord into a pantry, a letter in block capitals, a sign in eyeliner at an airport — and a gas station where something goes public.

s01.slug: FRIDAY · 4:50 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT ROOM
body: The holy day is going out of the front window a few minutes at a time. By a quarter to five the sky over the roofs across Glenwood is the same gray as the snow along the curb — two inches fell before breakfast, and it has been plowed against and walked on ever since — and the tree is lit anyway, every bulb. One more week.

At ten it was Mary, Mother of God at St. Brigid’s, half the South Side in the pews in last night’s clothes. The first reading was Numbers — *The LORD bless you and keep you!* — and Fr. Dom, who has never in his life been able to leave a blessing alone, put his hand up over the pews at the end and gave it to them again. Gina slept on Jack’s shoulder through the naming in Luke with her mouth a little open, and woke for the Creed and got every word.

Now it’s Pasadena on the television. Frank is in his chair in the Buckeyes sweatshirt he takes out one day a year and which is, by now, mostly lint. Ma has the dish towel over her shoulder and the arm of his chair for a seat. Gina has the arm of the couch and the Flip. Rosie is on her stomach on the rug with the blue crab under one elbow and a bowl under the other, and in the window chair, under Theo’s cashmere, Nonna sits up straight with her beads in one hand and a spoon in the other and her eyes on the pot.

The pot is on the coffee table on a trivet, brown and plain and steaming up the lamp: lentils. The rule is older than the house. First meal of the year, one spoon each, *per i soldi*, a lentil for every coin you want. Ma goes around the room with the ladle. Jack’s goes in. Gina’s goes in, with a face. Ma tastes her own for salt, because a rule is a rule but it’s also her pot, and Nonna, who won’t touch her own until everyone else has taken theirs, watches each spoon from the bowl to the mouth.

Rosie doesn’t eat hers. She counts them out onto the rim of her bowl, a lentil at a time, and sorts them by value. “That’s a quarter. That’s a dime. That one,” holding it up to the lamp, “is Canadian, so it’s only worth some.”
From his chair, eyes on the screen, Frank says, “Don’t let the hall see that. They’ll want dues.”
“That’s going in the documentary,” Gina says.

Ma comes to Frank’s chair last. He holds up his bowl without taking his eyes off Pasadena. “Two.” Ma looks at the bowl. She gives him two. In the window chair, Nonna’s eyes follow the second spoon down.

It’s a good first half, from where they sit. Pryor runs like he means it. Oregon comes out in a uniform that Frank looks at for some time before asking if they lost a bet, and everybody in the stands is in shirtsleeves in January, which he also takes personally. He coaches the set in single words — *Wrap. Eyes. Low.* — and Gina keeps the Flip on him through all of it. “For the extras,” she says, when he points out the lens. By the second quarter Nonna is asleep with the spoon still upright in her fist, in case there’s another round.

At the half the bands come out onto the grass, and Jack gets up. “Where are you going?” Gina says. “Garage.” “It’s *halftime*.” “That’s why.” He takes the Carhartt down off its hook in the hall and gets an arm into it. From there he can see the whole room: Rosie building her coins into a tower for the second half, and Frank at the halftime numbers, going down the column with his lips moving, checking the math.

The space heater takes its time coming up orange. The colored lights are still strung along the pegboard, one more week of them, so the garage looks like a bar that closes Wednesday, and the Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall with its door shut. Over the bench the 1964 program hangs in its freezer bag. Through the side door, thin and far off, a marching band in Pasadena. Jack sits down on the duct-taped chair with the RAZR open on his knee.

All week it has been her calling: a whisper on the back steps at midnight, the register and the ice machine, the river at dawn. He hasn’t dialed once. Tonight he does, because at his midnight he answered somebody else first, on purpose, and an hour later the clock turned over in his hand with her name on it, and he has been hearing it turn ever since.
She picks up already talking to somebody else. “Hold on. Hold on — Mama, it’s — *hold on*.” A door, and the house on her end drops by half. “You called *me*.”
“I called you.”

“Jack Costigan called me on the telephone. On purpose. Mémère, write down the date.” Behind her an old woman says something in French that doesn’t sound like anybody writing anything down. “She says it’s the first. She says she’ll remember it without a pencil.”
“Happy New Year, Jack. Again.”

It’s ten after five on Dupre Street, and she gives it to him in pieces. The black-eyed peas and the cabbage have been on the stove since noon. Every light in the house is still on from last night. Her daddy is in the den with the Sugar Bowl pregame, three hours early, to be sure of his chair. “Sweeping is forbidden till tomorrow. Mama’s walking around the kitchen with her hands behind her back so she won’t pick up the broom.”

Four minutes of nothing. Whether a lentil is a vegetable — “It’s a *legume*, Jack. Don’t you call my peas’ cousin a vegetable on New Year’s Day” — and whether Ohio State can keep it up, and whether Mémère, who has been told twice, will ever accept that there is a state called Oregon. Somebody wants her in the kitchen, two somebodies, and there are plates to carry.
“Call me back when y’all win.”
“And if we lose?”
“Then don’t,” Lena says, and the kitchen on Dupre Street comes up loud around her — pans, her mother, a radio — and then it’s the garage again, the heater, the band through the door.

At twenty past eight it’s over: Ohio State 26, Oregon 17, and everybody in Pasadena in their shirtsleeves going home happy. Frank turns the set off with the remote, lays the remote on the arm of his chair, and gives the whole review.
“Pryor.”
In the window chair Nonna wakes with her spoon still upright in her fist and wants to know who won. Rosie gets up off the rug and goes and shows her, in coins.

s02.slug: SATURDAY · 3:40 PM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE, THE CONFESSION LINE
body: The line for Saturday confession at St. Brigid’s runs from the box back along the side aisle to the third Station. It is short, and everyone in it has the sober, overdrawn look of the first week of January. Three women in good wool coats stand in order of age. Behind Jack a Holy Name man in a windbreaker has written out his list on the back of a Giant Eagle receipt, and he reads it over with his lips moving, and each time the line advances he tucks it into his breast pocket, as if the priest might frisk him on the way in.

Up the nave the garland is going brown at the tips where it meets the pillars. In the crib the three kings stand a pew-length from the manger, where the Altar Society has been walking them a little closer every morning since the twenty-sixth; they get there tomorrow. Over the middle door of the box the small light is green.
“You’re Frank Costigan’s,” the Holy Name man says behind him, in the low voice the whole parish uses in line, the kind that carries to the Stations. “The college one.”
“Yes, sir.”
“They keep you busy out there?”
“Some.”
The man nods and pats the pocket with the receipt in it. “Mine’s mostly the Browns,” he says. “But I got it organized.”
“Does that help?”
“Helps Father. He likes to know where to start.”
What Jack has in him he has had since Tuesday before light: a phone, a basement, two hours and seven minutes, and a battery that quit before he did. Nine days since he knelt in this box.
The third woman comes out of the left curtain pulling her gloves on, and the line takes its step, and Jack is next, with nothing to read.

choices.key: The Saturday after New Year’s you went to confession at St. Brigid’s.
response: The curtain on the left hangs still. Over the middle door the light stays green, the way it has since before Jack was baptized, and he takes the cloth in his fist and goes in.

choices.text: *Not here. Carry it to Father Osei, the one who knows the whole thing.*
choices.key: The Saturday after New Year’s you left the confession line at St. Brigid’s to wait for Father Osei.
response: He steps out of the line. It takes less than a second, and the line doesn’t notice; it was never going to. He has his reasons, in order. Father Osei has heard him every Saturday since September, so it would take an hour to tell Father Dom what Osei already knows. Two Saturdays isn’t long. And a man ought to confess a thing to the one who already has the rest of it.
Behind him the Holy Name man folds his receipt in half and takes Jack’s place without looking up, and the left curtain falls on him.
On the steps it has started to snow on the salt.

choices.text: *Go home. Ma’s got the oven on.*
choices.key: The Saturday after New Year’s you left the confession line at St. Brigid’s and went home.
response: He steps out of the line, and the line closes up behind him like water. Past the Stations; the side door; the salt. It is a quarter to four. Ma has something in the oven, and by the end of the block he can smell it, which is the reason he gives himself.
Behind him in the church the light over the box stays green for whoever is next.

s02a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:55 PM · ST. BRIGID’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: In the box it is dark enough that the burn in the screen is the brightest thing: a cigarette hole from before Vatican II, brown-ringed, the size of a dime, letting through a coin of yellow from Father Dom’s side that moves across the grille when he does. The radiator in the wall that was ticking on Christmas Eve is cold today, and the quiet where the ticking was is louder. The chair creaks. The cough drop clicks. The little door slides open.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been nine days since my last confession.”
“Nine days. That’s a respectable interval,” Father Dom says. “Go ahead.”
“There’s a girl. On the phone.” Jack says it to the grille. “We said — what we’d do.” The cough drop stops. “I said it too.”
“Did you do anything?”
“No, Father. Just said.”
“Just,” Father Dom says.
*Just* has held Jack’s weight all week. In here it turns out to be a card table. In the Carhartt’s inside pocket the RAZR is on vibrate, and vibrate, in a confessional, is not the same as silent.
“Who ended it?”
“The battery, Father. On my phone. It died.”
“Thank God for Motorola,” Father Dom says. “Then notice it wasn’t you.”
Out in the line a receipt is being unfolded. The cough drop goes over to the other cheek, and the dime of light holds still on the brass.
“Anything else?”
“Another picture. I opened it.”
“That’s everything, Father.”
“Christmas Eve you asked me to pray for her,” Father Dom says. “I have been. Skye.”

The chair creaks while he finds the knee. “I’ll tell you what that screen’s for. So a man can say a thing in the dark and it goes to God and not to the fella on this side of the cloth. I don’t get to keep it. I don’t get to hold it over you in the parking lot.” “You found another use for a voice in the dark.”
Jack has nothing to say to that. There is nothing on the kneeler to say it to.

“*Just said.*” Father Dom turns it over once more. “I stand up there Sundays and say a sentence over a piece of bread, and the building is there for that. God said *let there be light* and didn’t lift a hand. Words aren’t the small part, Jack. And you’ve got a voice. I’ve been listening to it since you were a third-grader losing your place at the school Mass. Priests and con men carry the same equipment; the difference is where they point it. Saying it out loud is a power. You pointed yours at the wrong end of the line. This is the right end. Say it here.”
“For your penance, the Joyful Mysteries. Slowly. Tomorrow, with somebody who’ll keep your count.” A pause for the knee. “Now. She’ll call, or you will. What happens when it starts?”

response: “I’ll hang up when it starts,” Jack says.
“Hang it up before it starts. You know the sound it makes before.”

The Act of Contrition goes into the cloth by heart, and on the other side Father Dom’s hand rises. *I absolve you.* Jack doesn’t see the cross, only the cloth stirring with it and the dime of light jumping on the grille and settling. “Go in peace.” “Thanks be to God.” He draws the curtain back on the Holy Name man, already on his feet with the receipt out, and they trade a nod, one parishioner to another. On the steps the snow has started on the salt, fine as flour. Back in the nave the three kings stand their pew-length from the crib with their gifts held out to a manger still a pew away.

body: The kitchen has gone to its late shape: the supper dishes standing in the rack, the light over the stove, the window over the sink black with the yard in it. Gina is at the table with a magazine she turns a page of every few minutes without reading. Rosie is under the table in her nightgown with the blue crab, because it’s break and nobody has the strength. From the front room comes the late bowl game, two schools Frank has no feelings about, and Frank having them anyway. Jack has a glass of milk and *The Moviegoer* shut by his elbow, finished.
At twenty to ten the wall phone by the pantry rings, which on Glenwood Avenue at that hour means somebody died or somebody’s drunk.
Ma gets it with the dish towel over her shoulder. “Costigan’s.”
“Yes, this is she.” And Jack watches his mother’s face go from the face she answers the phone with to another one altogether. “*Lena.*”
Gina’s magazine goes down flat on the table.
After that it’s ten minutes of his mother’s half. He gets no more than that, and he gets all of it.
“I know, honey. I know. He told us everything. Godmother — that’s a big job. When? … Tomorrow. During the *game*? Well. That’s the South, I guess.”

She turns to the window over the sink to have the rest. “The — the *coffee*?” Her eyes come across the kitchen and land on Jack. “*That* was you. Honey, it was very good coffee. He told me *a friend*.” She listens. “Well, that’s what he said.”
“The book, yes. You *wrote* in it. I didn’t read it. I saw.”
“Him? He eats standing up. I don’t know where he gets it. His father sits.” And she laughs at the window, at something on the other end Jack will never get to hear.
From the front room, over the game: “*La suora?*”

Ma, with the receiver against her chest: “*Sì, Ma.*” Nothing else comes from the chair. Across the table Gina is mouthing things at him, enormous, a word at a time, none of which he is going to dignify.

Rosie comes out from under the table and stands at Ma’s hip until she can’t be ignored, and gets the phone in both hands. “Hi. This is Rosie.” She listens with her face turned up. “You’re welcome.” And, because a godmother ought to know: “I got a crab for Christmas. *Callinectes sapidus.*” She listens again, nods at the phone, and hands it back up. “She says that means beautiful swimmer,” she tells the kitchen, and goes back under the table.
Ma puts the receiver to her collarbone and looks at her son.
“She called *information*.”
Jack puts down his milk.
“She wants you.” Ma holds it out to him and doesn’t let go of it yet. “I don’t know why.”

The cord is the long one, the one that reaches the stove and the sink and, with a pull, the pantry, and it has been stretched that way so many times it hangs in a loop when nobody’s using it. He takes it into the pantry and pulls the door to on it, and the cord keeps the door an inch open. In here it’s the canned tomatoes, a shelf of them, and Nonna’s jars of peppers in oil with the dates on masking tape, and the bulb on its chain. He pulls the chain. Out in the kitchen Gina’s chair scrapes, and her socks go off toward the stairs.
There’s a click on the line. Upstairs, an extension coming off its hook.
“G,” he says.
Click.
“Hey,” he says, to the tomatoes.

“Hey yourself. I’m in my old room. On my old bed, under a poster of a horse I don’t remember ever wanting. Mama keeps it like a shrine: my debate trophies, my First Communion crucifix, a picture of me at the state finals in a blazer with shoulders like a linebacker. It’s a museum of a very loud child.” Something on her end chirps, a little electronic cricket. “That’s Mama’s cordless. It does that.” From somewhere down the hall in her house, music with a lot of bass in it, and then somebody making it stop.
“You called my *house*.”
“I wanted to hear your house.”
“And?”
“Your mama answers like she’s going to bill somebody.” The cricket. “I liked her. I liked her a lot. She asked me did I eat.”
“What’d you tell her?”

“The truth. Red beans at noon and a praline at four, and something green tomorrow, I promise. She said that’s what you say too.” Down the hall the bass comes back on, lower. “Now tell me where you are.”

So he tells her. The pantry: a shelf of Hunt’s, Nonna’s peppers in oil with the year on masking tape, a box of Christmas candles nobody lit, the bulb on its chain. The kitchen through the inch of door, the stove light, the refrigerator going. His father in the front room explaining a holding call to two schools that can’t hear him. His grandmother asleep in her chair by the window. Rosie under the table with a crab.
“That’s the house,” she says. “That’s what I wanted.”
Tomorrow is the font: Our Lady of the Holy Rosary, the afternoon. “Father scheduled it during the game. Daddy has written to the Archbishop.” And the gown. She tells it to him from the bed, low.

“It’s Grandmère’s. She made it for Luc, in 1985. Every stitch — there’s a lily on the hem you can only see if you know it’s there. Every one of us wore it. The twins had to take turns at the font, and Josie went first, because she was louder.” The cricket. “It was in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge for the storm. That’s why we have it. It’s the only thing Grandmère made that we still have. It smells like the chest. I ironed it myself tonight. I didn’t want anybody else to touch it.”
“How’d it come out?”

“Perfect. I used a pillowcase in between. Mama stood in the door and watched me like I was cutting the red wire.” And in the same breath as the ironing: “Luc asked Wes to stand in the back. He said he’d come to the house after. Not the church.”
She leaves it there. Jack looks at the dates on Nonna’s jars, and she goes on.
“Do you know what a godmother is, Jack? Actually. Not the dress.”
“You hold the candle.”

“You hold the candle, and you stand up in front of God and the whole parish and say that if Tess and Beau can’t, you will. That you’ll see she’s raised in it. Prayers at night, the sacraments, the hard parts — whatever they can’t do is yours.” The cricket. “Luc says it’s like co-signing on a car. Mama hit him with a spoon. But he’s not wrong. I sign tomorrow and I don’t get to un-sign. She’ll be forty and I’ll still be on the paper.”
“Jack. I need you to be the priest.”
“I’m not qualified.”

“You’re Catholic and you’re awake. In this house that’s a vocation.” The cricket. “Father is going to ask me the questions in front of God and Mama and everybody, and I have to answer them for her, because she can’t, and if I get a word wrong in front of Mémère I’ll have to move to Lafayette. She’ll be in the front pew with her lips going, half a word ahead of me, so she can catch me if I fall. I’ve never been responsible for anybody’s soul before. I can’t keep a fern alive.”

She has the booklet from the rectory; pages turn on her end. She reads him his part and then hers, so he’ll know where to stop, and he writes it on the back of Ma’s grocery pad with the pencil on the string.
*Do you reject Satan?* *I do.*
*And all his works?* *I do.*
*And all his empty promises?* *I do.*

Then the Creed, cut into its three questions — *Do you believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth?* — and the Son, born and crucified and risen, and the Spirit, the Church, the saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting, each of them with its *I do*. She whispers all of it from her childhood bed, and she’s surer on every one.
“Now you,” she says. “Ask me.”

choices.text: *Ask them straight, the way Father Dom would.*
choices.key: The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you asked her the promises straight.
response: He asks them straight, low, under the bulb, the way Father Dom would: no voice put on, just the questions. *Do you reject Satan?* *I do.* She answers every one, all the way down to the life everlasting.
“Again.”
He asks them again. She gets them all. The third time through, she doesn’t need the booklet, and he doesn’t need the grocery pad.

choices.key: The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you asked her the promises in Latin.
response: “*Abrenuntias Satanae?*”

“*Abrenuntio.*” Not a hitch. *Et omnibus operibus eius? Abrenuntio. Et omnibus pompis eius? Abrenuntio.* She knows the old rite cold, every *Credis* and every *Credo*, and gets to the end of it faster than he can find his place in his own church Latin.
She’s laughing by the end. “You say it like a Steelers fan.”
“Take that back.”
“Forty miles from Pittsburgh, Jack. It gets in the water.”

choices.key: The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you said the promises with her.
response: He asks the first, and she answers. He asks the second, and she answers. He asks the third — *And all his empty promises?* — and her *I do* comes, and under it, low, his.
When he starts the Creed she gets the first word of her answer wrong, and stops, and starts it over. She isn’t quite level through the first two questions. By the third she is. *I do.*

body: At 10:41 the cordless dies in the middle of her sentence — she is telling him about Josie’s First Communion, and the veil, and the cat — and there’s nothing on the line, and then the dial tone.

He stands under the bulb with the dial tone for half a minute. Then he reaches around the door and hangs the receiver on its hook, and it rings under his hand before it has settled, and he has it up again before his mother can get out of her chair in the front room.
“I’m standing in the hall with it plugged into the wall like a lamp,” Lena says. “Mama’s cordless is older than Remy, and Remy’s older than God.”

He finished *The Moviegoer* New Year’s night, after the game, and he didn’t read the end first. She wants to know that before anything. Her pencil goes all the way to the last page. He followed it for two days, *no* and *ha* and *oh, honey* down the middle of the book, and at the very end, under the children in the car, in a harder pencil than the rest: *wrong*.
“So you agree with me,” he says.
“About what? You haven’t said anything yet.”

“It’s a surrender. He spends the book looking — for God, for the thing behind the thing, whatever he calls it that week — and then it’s Ash Wednesday and he marries Kate and signs up for medical school and the looking stops. And the book wants me to call that grace. It’s a guy who got tired and took the job.”
“That’s what she said. The girl with the pencil. Word for word, and she was very proud of herself.” A door on her end. “I was seventeen. I argue with her too.”
“So argue.”

“He doesn’t stop looking, Jack. He stops looking *by himself*.” She’s going now, the long sentence building to its verdict. “The looking by himself was the sickness. It’s right there at the front, Kierkegaard — the despair that doesn’t know it’s despair. A man alone in a movie house in Gentilly looking for God is a man who has decided God is something you find on your own, like a parking space. And at the end he’s got Kate, and he’s got those children asking him about their brother, and he *answers* them. A man who quit doesn’t answer children.”

“Then where’s God in it? He looks for Him the whole book, and at the end he won’t say the word. Grace is supposed to *happen* to you. Paul on the road. Augustine in the garden — *take and read*. It knocks you down in the dirt. It doesn’t sign you up for medical school.”

“Grace perfects nature, Costigan. It doesn’t cancel it. You keep wanting God to show up like a fire truck.” Down the hall a door, and her voice drops back to the hall’s size. “Most people He gets the regular way. A wife. A job. Some children who need somebody to answer them. Percy didn’t put God in a speech. He put Him in the car.”
“That’s Ohio talk. Get a job, get married, don’t make a fuss.”
“That’s *Thomas* talk, and you know it. You only like the dirt because you’ve never had to live in it after.”
“And the grace part?”
“Is the part where he lets them in the car.”
“You wrote *wrong* in pencil, though.”
“I write everything in pencil, Costigan. I’m Catholic. I expect to be corrected.”
Out on the kitchen table, through the inch of door, the book lies shut by his milk with her *wrong* in it.
“My brother asked me something at Christmas,” he says. “I can’t answer it yet.”
“The truck?”
“Before that.”

She doesn’t ask what. “Then don’t answer it till you can.” The cordless chirps in the hall, plugged in or not. “Some things you have to grow into. Lucille’s going to be swimming in that gown tomorrow, and it’s still hers.”

They go on to things that don’t matter, which matter. He tells her about Nonna’s lentils, a spoon each for the money, and Rosie stacking hers into quarters on the rim of the bowl. “For *money*? We do cabbage. Y’all are smaller about it.” And about Rosie: “That child is going to run the Vatican Bank, and it’ll be the first time the books balance.” She has taken the cordless back to bed — “It’s had its rest” — and it chirps at her every few minutes, and she ignores it like a little brother. She’s in the middle of what Remy did on the levee at midnight, not with anything that lights, Mama’s rule held, with something worse, when she says, lightly, in the same breath:
“How’s California?”

choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her: three hours behind.
response: “Three hours behind.”
“It always was,” she says, and goes on to the rest of Remy.

choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her: far away.
response: “Far away.”
“Good,” she says, and goes on to the rest of Remy.

choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her you weren’t thinking about California tonight.

It’s true tonight. It’s true in this pantry with the cord through the door.

body: At 11:25 the cordless chirps three times fast and gives up for good. This time when he hangs up it takes a minute, and when the wall rings again the line is nearer, cleaner, her own phone.
“Mama’s cordless,” Lena says, “has given its life for the Church.”

The house has gone up while they talked. The game is off in the front room; Ma said goodnight through the pantry door and he said it back with his hand over the mouthpiece. He comes out and sits down on the kitchen floor with his back against the cabinet under the sink, as far as the cord will reach, and puts his legs out on the linoleum. The light over the stove is the only one on. Under the floor the furnace is running; he can feel it come up through the tiles.

Nothing that matters, for most of an hour. The 8-Ball is on her nightstand, and she shakes it once about tomorrow and reads it to him: *You may rely on it.* “I shook it one time. I’m a godmother, Costigan. I don’t cheat.” Remy, somewhere in her house, singing along to something, wrong. Whether godmothers get a pew. (“The front one. Daddy already measured it.”) Whether a godmother can wear red. Mémère says no. Lena is wearing white anyway. “Mémère says that’s showing off. I said it’s the *Church’s* color, Mémère, take it up with the Pope.” Lucille is at Tess and Beau’s tonight; tomorrow she gets handed over at the church door, gown and all. “She won’t remember one minute of it,” Lena says. “That’s what the paper’s for. Everybody else remembers it for her.”
“Where are you now?”
“The kitchen floor.”

“Jack Costigan, get up off that floor, you’ll catch your death.” Her mother’s exact sentence, he’d bet the truck on it. He doesn’t get up. He tells her the furnace is under him and the stove light is on and the whole house is asleep except the refrigerator, and she says that’s the saddest thing she ever heard and the nicest, and to stay there, then, if he’s going to be stubborn.
A little before midnight she yawns in the middle of a word and denies it.
“I have to sleep. I have somebody’s soul at two o’clock.” A rustle, the sheet or the horse. “Come back, Youngstown.”
“I’m coming back.”
“Good. Goodnight, Jack.”

Two hours on his mother’s phone, and she never once said Julian’s name. Julian is staying in that house — in Remy’s room, the last Jack heard, with his shoes lined up under the bed. Jack listened for it from the first word.
The cord lies across the linoleum from the wall to his hand.

body: The kings came in the night. At the eight o’clock they stand at the foot of the manger with their arms full of gold-foil boxes, the gold one’s crown on crooked, and somebody from the Altar Society has combed the straw. Father Dom reads Matthew in white with the cough drop going — the star, the scribes, Herod asking them to bring him word — and gives three sentences for a homily. “They came the long way,” he says. “They went home a different one, and Matthew doesn’t tell you what the dream was. Sometimes you just try the other door.” On the steps Rosie, who was lent Pop’s Timex for the purpose, reports forty-one seconds. A parish record, she says. Gina says nobody was keeping one.

In the lot at Trumbull the plows have left their gray bank along the fence again, and the same wind comes across the fields. The radio has a Cleveland pregame show on, three hours before kickoff because it is Cleveland: two men and a caller with a grievance about the Jaguars’ secondary. Gina and Rosie are out and stamping on the salt.

Ma drove today. She took the keys out of Frank’s hand at the curb on Glenwood without a word, and he rode up in the passenger seat with his hat on his knee, and there is no engine for him to sit with. He is first out.
Ma comes around the hood with the Folgers can against her hip. Across the lot Frank is a step ahead of her.
Inside, the officer at the desk says “Maria” and then “Frank,” and doesn’t look at the clipboard for either.

The paper tree is gone from over the microwave. In its place on the cinderblock, about as high as a short man can reach, is a star cut out of a yellow legal pad, five points, one of them bent. Danny is at the table already, in the state blues, facing the door. When Frank comes through it behind Ma, he stands.
His hands are at his sides this time, not folded. He is on his feet before the officer on the platform has looked up.
Ma bends and kisses him on both cheeks, the Italian way, and sits. Frank, in the sport coat again, takes the bolted chair across from his son and looks over Danny’s head at the cinderblock.
“Somebody’s been to Bethlehem,” he says.

Danny turns in his chair to look at the star, and back. “Chaplain’s kings are this afternoon,” he tells the table. “Reggie, a guy from Lorain, and the chaplain’s assistant, in bedsheets. Reggie won’t say which king he is. He says I’ll tell.”
“Is there a camel?” Rosie asks.
“There’s a mop,” Danny says. “It’s very patient.”
“Ma says Gina’s writing me a word she can’t spell,” he adds.
“I can spell it,” Gina says. “I spelled it. I mailed it Wednesday.”
“It’ll get here. Everything gets here. It just doesn’t get here in the order it left.” He sits back, and crosses his arms over the state blues. “They win today, that’s four.”
“They’ll win,” Frank says.
Danny looks at him. Down the table Ma finds the legal-pad star very interesting.
Gina does the first run to the machines with a fistful of Ma’s quarters and comes back with a honey bun for everybody, cellophane crackling. Rosie holds hers up to the star, for reasons of her own.

Ma stands with the can and says “Frank,” and takes him to the machines. He is better at them now. There is no boy in a clip-on tie to supervise, and he doesn’t need one; he reads the front of the coffee machine over his glasses, feeds in the quarters himself, one at a time, and when the creamer comes it stops when it should. Ma stands behind him with the can in the crook of her arm and watches him do it.
Rosie and Gina take the last of the quarters to the toy corner. Danny keeps his voice under the room.
“Nonna do the lentils?”
“A spoon each, for the money. Pop held out for two.”
Danny looks across the room at the man in the sport coat, bent to the coffee machine with his reading glasses on.
“Holding out for a better offer,” he says. “So when do I see you, Professor?”
“May.”
“May.” Danny turns it over. “Bring the rich one. And get your hair cut.”
“Ma says that.”
“Ma’s right.”
“What’s coming this month?” Danny says. Jack sends him one book a month, used, and a separate sheet for the margins.
“I haven’t picked.”
“Pick short. Reggie wants a turn.”
“Reggie reads?”
“Reggie listens. I do the voices.” He says it without a trace of shame. “The Housman I did as a Browns announcer.”

Frank comes back across the room with a cup in each hand, held out from his body, and sets one in front of Danny. It’s pale. The torn packets are in his fist. Danny looks at the cup, and at his father, and picks it up and drinks.
“Thanks, Pop.”

When the officer calls time the room gets up in one scrape of chairs. Danny does his family one at a time: Rosie, swung once; Gina, who says *ow*; Ma, whom he lifts clear of the linoleum; Jack, with a hand on the back of his head and, in his ear, “Professor.” Frank has his hand out across the table, as he did a week ago. Danny looks at it. Then he comes around the end of the table and puts both arms around his father, sport coat and all.
Frank’s hands go out from his sides and hang there. Then one comes up and lands between Danny’s shoulder blades, and the other follows it. Two pats. Then not patting.
Out in the lot, with her coat back on, Gina points the Flip at the fence and the wire along the top of it. “B-roll,” she says. “Quiet on the set.” Rosie, who still has the Timex, times it.

At twenty past eleven the house is in bed and the RAZR goes off in his hand in the dark kitchen, where he has been standing at the open refrigerator for no reason. He takes it to the top of the basement stairs, where it gets its two bars, and answers it there, and carries it down with him. At the bottom he pulls the string on the bulb. Gina’s chair is at the Dell where she left it. He turns it on the concrete so its back is to the furnace, and sits.
“Hi,” Skye says. “I’m on my mother’s balcony with a blanket and a glass of her wine, and you’re in trouble.”
Behind her, through glass, a bird says *momager*.
“The parrot,” she says. “My mother’s inside on the other line with the network. She’s always on with the network. Pasadena. Friday. You said seventy.”
“It was close.”
“It was *not* seventy. I asked a man who was there. He was wearing a fleece, Jack. A *fleece*. I’m docking you a point.”
“From a seven.”
“You’re a six. Sixes don’t get to argue.”
The blanket moves; a chair creaks out on the balcony. “So. News. My people want lunch.”
“Your people.”

“My mother — Debbie, she manages me — and Corinne, who’s my publicist, which means she manages the managing. Sunday. In town. I’ll get you after your church.” She takes a drink. “They want to see you before anybody sees you.”
“Who’s going to see me?”

“Everybody, in February, if Corinne gets her way. There’s a plan. There’s a carpet. The two of us get *spotted* going into something, by a man from a magazine who just happens to be standing right there.” A sound into the glass, half a laugh and half the other thing. “I’m mortified. I’m having a wonderful time. Wear the blazer from the rain.”
“It’s my only blazer.”
“That’s why it’s the one. And I’m driving up Thursday, back into Sol’s. The heater’s broken. Sol says it’s character.” The chair again. “Now. Rehearsal.”
Her voice goes clipped and quick — a woman walking between two meetings with a phone at each ear. “Where’s Youngstown?”
“Ohio.”
“Is Ohio a *choice*?”

He laughs, and she’s already gone on. “That’s Corinne. Corinne will Google you before the bread comes. Now my mother.” A breath, and somebody else comes up out of it: warm as a hotel lobby, younger than it ought to be, a hand on your arm in every word. “Jack. *Jack.* Sit, sit, sit. Are your people *in* something?”
“My father’s on a list at the union hall.”
“Is that a *network*?” And she’s herself again, fast. “Notes. Don’t say *ma’am*, she’s thirty-nine on paper. Don’t look at the bread. She’ll think you’re poor. You are poor. Don’t look at the bread.”
“I won’t look at the bread.”

“Here’s the table.” The chair scrapes; she’s sitting forward. “Corinne wants a story she can control. She doesn’t care if it’s a good one, she cares if it holds still. My mother wants to be liked more than she wants to like you, so let her — it costs you nothing, and she’ll think it was her idea. And the two of them, all through lunch, through the bread and the little spoons, are going to be trying to find out one thing.”
“What.”
“What you want from me.”
The Dell’s dark screen gives him back a guy under a bare bulb who is going to have to answer that over soup.
“Also,” Skye says, “I read your Matthew.”
“My Matthew.”

“You said your grandmother’s tree comes down after the Epiphany. So on Sunday I looked it up on my phone, in a Coffee Bean on Ventura, next to a man writing a screenplay about a dolphin. And Herod is a showrunner. A jealous one. He hears there’s a new lead in town, and he calls the visitors in *secretly* — it says secretly — and he wants the exact date the star showed up. He’s doing the schedule. And then it’s, go find the kid, tell me where he’s shooting, so I can come and *pay my respects*.”
“That’s not —”

“The Magi are the first fans. They see one star and cross a desert with presents for a kid they’ve never met. And then they get a dream and go home by another way.” The glass, the blanket. “That’s a publicist’s move, Jack. They ducked the press.”

He sits forward in Gina’s chair with his elbows on his knees. “They weren’t supposed to be in it,” he says. “That’s the thing about them. No covenant, no prophets, no promises. Foreigners with a star chart. They came anyway. The Church keeps a day for them — for everybody who shows up from outside the story.”
The balcony chair creaks. “That’s good,” Skye says. “That’s annoyingly good. I’m going to have to come to one of these.”
“One of what?”
“Your day for the people from outside.” A sip. “Who picked February?”
“What?”
“That’s my question. In these stories nobody asks who picks the date. They just *run*.”
He hears the foot of the glass touch down on the concrete out there.

“I hate it,” she says. “The carpet. The man from the magazine who happens to be there. You in the blazer, looking kidnapped. I’ve never decided one thing about my own face.” The blanket. “I’d like to be the one who tells people about you.”
Over his head somebody crosses the kitchen in socks for a glass of water, and runs the tap, and goes back up.
When she comes back she’s lower, closer to the phone. “I’m not saying anything else tonight. My mother’s on the other side of a sliding door and you’re on a payment plan.”
“Since when?”
“Since the furnace. Saturday. After I pick you up — which I am.”
“I’ve got a thing at nine. My roommate’s people.”

“Ted’s thing.”
“Then I have you from the airport to Ted’s thing.” She counts it off, seven fifty-two to nine. “An hour. I’ve done whole episodes in less.”

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:15 AM · THE FRONT ROOM → 4:40 PM · THE SIDE YARD AND THE GARAGE
body: The front window is going from black to gray at a quarter past seven when the tape in the kitchen clunks over to its other side. It’s Nonna’s cassette, the carols a cousin in Warren taped off the radio before Danny was born, with a hiss on it older than any of the children. It goes back in the drawer under the toaster tonight, till next December. This morning it’s on the counter by the bread box, turned up to where the front room can have it, and Nonna, in her chair by the window with her beads in her lap, hums along a half beat behind.

Rosie’s stocking is the last one left on the mantel’s row of hooks, and in the night it has been filled: torrone in its white box, a clementine with the leaf still on, a fistful of chocolate coins in gold foil. She has the haul laid out on the rug and is briefing the blue crab. “The Befana was too busy sweeping to go with the kings,” Rosie says. “She said she’d catch up. Then she couldn’t find them. So now she goes to everybody’s house, in case the baby’s there.” In her chair, Nonna’s beads go on under the tape.

Jack comes down the stairs at twenty past with something swinging from his fist. It was hanging off the knob of the back bedroom door when he opened it, by its own cuff: one of Danny’s old tube socks, white, two blue stripes at the top, the heel worn nearly through, and heavy at the toe. The stairs are the one country Nonna hasn’t entered since the fall, so the Befana has had help. He tips the sock over into his palm. Black, glittering, a dozen lumps the size of walnuts, so convincingly coal that his first thought is the furnace.
“Nonna,” Gina says from the stairs behind him, hair in a knot, one sock on. “That’s *coal*.”
Nonna doesn’t look up from the beads. “*Dolce.*”
Rosie’s head comes up out of the stocking. “Jack was *bad*?”
Nonna lifts her chin and thinks it over.
“*Un pochino.*”
He breaks a corner off the biggest lump and lifts it toward his mouth, in front of her, since that appears to be what is required.
“Eat an egg first,” Ma says from the stove.
“It’s tradition, Ma.”
“So’s breakfast.” He eats it anyway. It’s sugar: black sugar, burnt at the edges, with a little anise at the back of it.
Frank, who has been in the kitchen doorway for a minute with his coffee, just seeing, says, “She gave me coal in ’81. It wasn’t sugar.”
Nonna, not looking up: “*Te lo meritavi.*”
“You brought me home at one,” Ma says, with her back to them.
Frank looks at his coffee. “Twice.”
Rosie, who has walked the three kings across the house since the twenty-sixth, a shelf at a time, from the far end of the bookcase, sets them down the last inch at the manger.

At twenty to five the day is done with Youngstown, and Frank and Jack are in the side yard taking down the Madonna’s lights. She has stood in her bathtub since before Danny was born, the paint worn pale at the nose, and there is snow lying in her cupped hands. Frank empties them first, with one glove, before he touches a bulb. Then the blue string comes off her in a long rope, and Jack coils it on his hand and elbow, as he was taught at eight. “Over,” Frank says. “Under.” The lesson has not been revised.
In the front-room window Nonna knocks once on the glass with a knuckle and, when they look, mouths it at them: *Finito.* Christmas is done.

In the garage the colored lights come down off the pegboard a loop at a time, and when the dead blue bulb comes level with the vise Frank stops and unscrews it. He holds it up under the overhead and looks at it, and drops it in the coffee can of drywall screws. From the sound, it has company. Behind them the pegboard is bare again except for the painted outlines of the tools, hammer and level and the long wrench, each in its black, waiting.

The Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall, as it has for as long as Jack has been tall enough to be told not to open it. Frank opens it. The little light comes on. Where the Stroh’s were, there is Canada Dry, standing in rows, green and gold. Frank takes out two. He sets one on the bench by Jack’s elbow and sits down on his bucket by the heater with the other. The duct-taped chair is under three boxes of lights, and the only other seat is the paint bucket at the end of the bench. On the bench the radio is on low, a man in Niles selling gutters.
“Hall called,” Frank says, and cracks his can. “Nothing yet.”

body: Monday he called from the garage at ten, with the radio off. Tuesday from the Giant Eagle lot with Ma’s list on the dash and the engine running for the heater. Tonight it’s the front porch, in the Carhartt, with the lights down off the house and Glenwood dark end to end except for the streetlights and the inflatable snowman across the street, which hasn’t heard. He dials, and she picks up on the first ring. He has called her every night since Sunday. He listens to every word she says for where she is.
Tonight is Twelfth Night, and she has news.
“It’s Carnival now,” Lena says. “Out here too.”

At dusk the Phunny Phorty Phellows rode the St. Charles streetcar in their masks, the way they do every Twelfth Night, throwing from the back, and one of them threw a strand of beads at Mémère on the neutral ground, and Mémère threw it back at him. “She told him she isn’t that kind of woman and it isn’t Mardi Gras yet. He caught it. He bowed to her off the back of a streetcar.”
And the first king cake, after supper, purple and green and gold sugar all over Mama’s good tablecloth — and she got the baby.

“It was in my second bite. A little plastic baby, about the size of a peanut, and I didn’t swallow it, which is how you know God loves me. Remy wanted it ruled a foul because I looked. I didn’t look. I *felt*.”
“Which means the next one’s mine,” she says. “I’m bringing it on the plane. On my lap. Laney says that’s a federal crime.”
“Is it?”
“It’s a *pastry*, Jack. It’s a Catholic pastry. Let them try.”

He tells her the lights came down today, and the house looks like it got caught without its coat. “We don’t take ours down,” she says. “We change the colors. Purple, green and gold by Sunday. Mémère says you don’t put away a party, you hand it to the next one.”
Down the block a storm door opens, and a man carries a dead tree out to the curb by its trunk and lays it down on the snowbank with the others.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull.

body: The mail on Glenwood comes at ten past one, and on Thursday it brings the gas bill, a Giant Eagle flyer with a ham on it, a card for Nonna from the Altar Society, and an envelope addressed in block capitals. TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION is stamped in the corner with a number underneath, and across the middle, in pencil gone over until it has dented the paper, MR. JACK COSTIGAN. The flap has been opened and sealed again at the institution with a strip of brown tape and somebody’s initials across the tape.

Jack is at the kitchen table over a bowl of Ma’s escarole soup. Gina brings the mail in off the porch, sees the corner of the top envelope, and is across the kitchen with it in her hand before the storm door has finished closing.
“That’s Danny. Give it.”
“No.”
“Jack.”
“It’s got my name on it.”
“Read it out loud,” Ma says from the stove.
“No.”
“I put the money on his stamps.”
“Ma.”
“I’m only saying.”
He reads it at the table. Gina sits across from him and reads it upside down, a skill she has had since she was six, with her arms folded and her lips moving.

body.title: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
body.text:
PROFESSOR. IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE.

Gina wrote me four pages about a yacht. A YACHT. She spelled it right, she put a box around it so I would know, I’m proud of her. Ma says underwear, Gina says bathing suit, I say is she blind. What did you tell her, you’re in a BAND. You can’t sing, I been in a car with you.

Reggie wants it known he was Balthazar on Epiphany and Balthazar brought the myrrh and the myrrh was a honey bun. Chaplain says the star on the wall counts as a star. I said it’s a legal pad. He said God works with what He’s got.

Pop came. The Browns won four straight. Tell Pop I said they’d lose and I was glad to be wrong, which is a first. Tell him next time black. He don’t have to make a thing of it.

The rich one sent books. Softcover. No staples. He called first to ask the rules, the C.O. told everybody.

Write me back. The real version. Not Gina’s. Eat something.
Push-ups 170.
—D.

body: “‘You can’t sing,’” Gina reads, with satisfaction. “‘I been in a car with you.’”
“I can sing.”
“Ma. Can he sing?”
“He sings like your father,” Ma says. “At the radio.”

In her chair in the kitchen doorway Nonna has been watching the envelope the whole time with her beads in her lap. “*Che dice?*” Gina leans over the back of her chair. “*Papà è entrato,*” she says. “*Due volte.*” Nonna says it back, *due volte*, and crosses herself, and that appears to be all the news she needs.
“He *spelled* yacht right,” Gina says. “I’m insulted.”
“Does he sound good?” Ma says. She hasn’t turned around.
“He sounds good, Ma.”
“Is he eating?”
“He told *me* to eat something.”
“Then he’s eating.”
Gina uncrosses her arms. “Well?” she says. “Blind or lied?”

body: The garage looks bigger with the lights down. The pegboard is bare except for the painted shapes of the tools that live on it, and the Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall with ginger ale in it, and the space heater has the near half of the room to itself. His duffel is already behind the seat of the truck for the morning. It’s half past nine on Dupre Street. He dials.

Her house is all suitcases. “Everybody’s flying somewhere. Mémère goes back to Breaux Bridge Sunday, the twins go back to school Monday, I’m Sunday at noon, and Josie has written an agenda for the airport. It has times on it. It has a column for *notes*.” A zipper, close by. “Mémère is packing me a jar of something for the dormitory. I asked what. She said *for the dormitory*. It’s not going to get through security. It’s not going to get through *Mama*.”

The king cake is in its box on the kitchen table, and nobody is allowed to look at it. “If the TSA wands my king cake I’m going to make a scene, Jack, and it’s going to be a Broussard scene. They’ll have to call the Coast Guard.”

Tess brought Lucille for supper and took her home asleep. “At the table she reached up and got my medal in her fist — just took it — and wouldn’t let go. Tess had to open her fingers one at a time. She has a grip like Daddy. Mémère crossed herself and said she’d known it all along, I don’t know what. She’s going to be a terror and I’m going to let her.”

“Is it snowing?” “It’s always snowing.” “I’ve seen snow twice in my life, Jack, and once it was hail.” He tells her his father is driving him to Pittsburgh in the morning, because Pittsburgh is cheaper, and she says only Ohio would drive to another state to leave it.

She wants to know what he did all day. Packed. Ma ironed his shirts, all four, and stacked them on Danny’s bed like the bed was going too. Rosie is making him a drawing for the door and has told him it’s a secret and that it’s a plane. “Then you act surprised,” Lena says. “Practice your face tonight. You have a terrible surprised face. I’ve seen it.”

She wants to know what he’s bringing back. He tells her: the Carhartt, a Tupperware of pizzelles Ma has packed in wax paper like they’re going to the moon, and a book he finished. She’s bringing the Greene for the plane, the one on Hale’s list. She has read it twice. “I hate her. I love her and I hate what she does. Hale’s going to make us fight about it in front of everybody, you know he is.” Remy goes back to Baton Rouge in the morning with a laundry bag the size of a person. Luc is on nights. The Saints play next Saturday, whoever wins Sunday, and her daddy is already sick to his stomach about both of them. “I’m watching it in the Fishbowl,” she says, “and y’all are going to be quiet, and nobody is going to say anything to me till it’s over.”
Then there’s a scuffle on her end, and a different voice altogether, old and French and much too close to the phone.
“*C’est le garçon d’Ohio?* You eating up there?”
“Yes, ma’am.”

“*Menteur.*” And then, as if it settles something: “When you come to New Orleans, you come to this house first.” And she’s gone, and it’s Lena again: “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian. I’m sorry. She does that.”
She lands Sunday at four. Laney’s getting her; Kevin’s driving, because Theo won’t let Laney touch his car. “Monday is Hale,” she says. “He’s got us at opposite ends.”
“For the safety of the others.”
“I’m taking the end by the window.”
“Julian gets back Sunday too,” she says. “Late. Tomorrow’s his birthday. He’s home in Oakland till Sunday.” A zipper. “So not this weekend.”
It’s the first time she’s said his name in a week.
“Yeah?”
“I’m going to see him Monday. Dinner, after Hale.” Something goes into the suitcase and gets pressed down. “Will you be around after? Monday night. Nine, ten.”
Monday night was spoken for on the basement phone, at half past one in the morning, by somebody who wasn’t asking. Jack looks at the bare pegboard.
“Probably not,” he says. “I’ve got a thing.”
“Okay,” Lena says. She doesn’t ask what thing. “Then call me after.”
“I haven’t been fair to him, Jack. I’ve known it a while. I’m going to fix it.”

It’s what she has always done. Where Julian is, when he lands, when he calls at ten his time — since September she has kept him posted, like a girl reading him the weather in a town he’ll never see. And under it, after a week of him dialing this number every night, he hears something being shut, gently, the way you’d shut a door on somebody asleep. *Then call me after*, as easy as that, like it costs her nothing; she didn’t even ask what the thing was, and she has never in her life not asked. She’s going home to make it right with Julian. She’s telling him so he’ll stop calling.

The trailer mirror at five in the morning. The hotel-bathroom mirror. The forty buttons. His own shirt in the back of a town car. The bedroom door at first light. The white tree.
The ocean, and the 10 on her hip.

body: He goes back up to the top and through them again, slower. A girl three time zones away has been holding a phone up to mirrors since the first week of December so a guy in a snow globe would have something to look at. The same girl docked him a point for Pasadena on the word of a man in a fleece. She read Matthew in a Coffee Bean so she could tell him Herod was a showrunner. Tomorrow night at 7:52 she is going to be at an airport in Santa Barbara, with an hour of him before Ted’s thing already counted. Somewhere around the town car he stops being a man lying in his brother’s room who got off the phone first, and he decides it — he can feel himself do it, like setting his feet before a lift — that he’s lucky. That he is, after all, a lucky man.
He’s smiling. At a screen the size of a stamp, in the dark. He puts the back of his wrist against his mouth like that’s going to do anything about it.
“Skye,” he tells the ceiling, which has heard worse from this bed.

He opens a new message and types what they do: *sat 7:52. if theres no marching band im getting back on the plane*. It’s good. It’s their usual. He looks at it, and takes it back out a letter at a time, and lies there with the empty box and the cursor going.

body: At ten to ten the duffel is by the front door and the zipper won’t close over the sandwiches. There are three, in foil, labeled in Ma’s capitals — PITTSBURGH TO DENVER. DENVER TO SANTA BARBARA. IN CASE. — because the airlines, she has told the front hall, do not feed anybody.

Nonna doesn’t get up. Jack goes to her chair, and it takes her a long time to find the twenty. The left pocket of the housedress first, then the right, then the left again: a tissue, a holy card, a butterscotch in cellophane, a bead come off something, and last the bill, folded to the size of a stamp. “*Per il viaggio*,” she says, and closes his fingers on it with her hand over his. Then her thumb goes to his forehead and makes the cross there, hard enough to keep, and she tells him close, in Calabrese, and he gets every word of it.
“*Prego per tutt’e due.*”
A breath later: “*Anche per Cassidy.*”
He kisses her cheek. She smells of Jergens and radiator. Her hand is still on his sleeve when Ma calls him from the side door.

Ma has the dish towel on her shoulder and the can in both hands. It’s the Café du Monde can from the cupboard, empty, washed, the lid pressed back on. “For the girl who called,” she says. “Tell her it was good coffee. Those words.” It goes into the duffel on top of the sandwiches, and Ma watches it go in.

Gina and Rosie are waiting on the side step, and the door’s spring bangs shut behind him. Rosie has a drawing in both hands, in her church shoes, for the plane: a plane, with Jack in a window, and in the next seat the blue crab, belted in, reading. Under the crab, in her best printing, CALLINECTES SAPIDUS. “So you’re not by yourself,” she says.
“Who gets the window?” Jack says.
“You. He’s on the aisle, in case.”
Gina has the Flip up and the red light on. “I’m keeping the tape. ‘Say things out loud.’ You’re on it forever.”
“Is that thing ever off?” Jack says.

“Not till the credits.” At the bottom of the step she puts her free arm around his neck, hard, and says into his ear, so low it’s mostly breath: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Then she’s back behind the lens as if she’d said nothing at all.

Frank takes the turnpike at the speed limit, in the right lane, through flurries that come down dry across the wipers, with KDKA low on the dash giving the Steelers their offseason. Frank, a Browns man, endures it.

At Departures the Silverado stops where the sign says nothing stops. A man in an orange vest opens a conversation with the windshield, and Frank rolls the window down two inches and says, “Thirty seconds,” and rolls it up. He gets the duffel from the back seat himself and puts it in Jack’s hand. Then the hug, one arm, hard, the other hand on the roof of the truck.
“Call your mother when you land,” he says. “She don’t sleep.”
Jack nods. He has turned for the doors when Frank adds it, in the same tone. “And tell the TV one the Browns won four straight. She’ll want to know.”

The doors open for him without being asked. When he looks back through the glass, the Silverado is still at the curb with its hazards going, the man in the vest at the window again, and Frank, well past his thirty seconds, explaining something to him with one hand.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny about the hall and the Cruze, and laughed, in there. Asked if the Saints girl sent the coffee. I said yeah. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass. New Year’s: two spoons of lentils, for the money. “Pryor.” Went in to see Danny again. “Four straight.” Twelfth Night we took the lights down, and the beer fridge is ginger ale now. At the curb in Pittsburgh: call your mother when you land. She don’t sleep.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.”

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab. Rosie’s midnight is at nine, off a tape Dad made in 1999. Pots and pans on the porch. Asleep by a quarter past with the spoon. Counted her New Year’s lentils out like coins. Put the three kings at the manger on the sixth. Drew me a plane with the crab in the next seat.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.*

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first.

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 7:52 PM · SANTA BARBARA AIRPORT, THE GATE
body: Denver was a seat over the wing and a man from Grand Junction asleep against his shoulder most of the way to the desert. At Santa Barbara there’s no jetway. They roll a stair up to the door in the dark, and he comes down it into air that’s soft and wet and smells of cut grass and jet fuel and, under both, the sea; and halfway down, the RAZR finds a bar and sets its clock back three hours. 7:52. He gets the whole evening over again.

Santa Barbara has no gate the way Denver has gates. It has a glass door off the apron and a rope beside it, and the people meeting the plane stand at the rope under a tile roof and a light full of moths, close enough to touch whoever comes in. He hears her before he sees her.
“JACK COSTIGAN.”

She is standing on a plastic chair at the rope, barefoot, in sunglasses — big black ones, at eight o’clock at night — holding up over her head a flap torn off a cardboard box. On it, in black eyeliner, gone over two and three times where the pencil gave out, in letters as tall as his hand:

body.title: A sign at the rope
body.text: OFFICIALLY

body: “YOUNGSTOWN, OHIO,” Skye tells the terminal, in case anybody missed it. A family of five with a stroller turns around. So does the man from Grand Junction. She has his blue oxford on, the sleeves rolled to the elbow, the tail down over her cutoffs, under a man’s flannel she hasn’t bothered to button, and her hair is down and full of salt.
“Why the sunglasses?” he says, when he gets to the rope.
“So nobody recognizes me.” She stays up on the chair, a head taller than him for once, and looks down at him over the top of them. “I said I wanted you in it. I lied. I wanted *me* in it.”

Up close she smells of sunscreen in January, and there’s sand dried on her ankles above the anklet, and the eyeliner she didn’t use on the sign is around her eyes, smudged, as if she’s been up since the sun.
“How’s the furnace?” she says. “Did it get its line?”
“Show me how your father held it.” He does: the phone out at arm’s length, the squint, the face doing nothing at all. She laughs until she has to put a hand down on the hood.

She comes down off the chair and over the rope in one move, and the duffel goes down on the tile, and she kisses him like there isn’t a terminal — long, the sunglasses pushed up into her hair, her hands in the back of his, his inside the flannel at the small of her back where the oxford is warm from her. Over her shoulder, by the belt, a girl from his flight in a Marisol sweatshirt has her phone up, sideways, at the height of her chest, very steady, the way you hold a phone when you aren’t calling anybody. He sees it. Then Skye’s hand closes in his hair, and he doesn’t see anything. “It’s an adverb,” she says against his mouth. “I looked it up. It modifies everything after it.”
A man in an airline vest, gray at the temples, not angry, a man who has worked this rope a long time: “Ma’am. The chair.”
She salutes him with the sign. “Sir, this man has come all the way from *Ohio*.”
“So he’s seen snow,” the man says. “The chair.”

Out at the curb the Saab is in the white zone with its hazards going: top up, the dent in the rear quarter panel catching the light from the doors, a surfboard sticking out of the back seat at an angle that has nothing to do with the law.

response: “I missed you.”
“I know,” Skye says. “It was on your face from the plane.” She takes his hand and walks him out the doors to the curb, swinging the sign. “Get in.”

“I had Sol check,” Skye says. “Two f’s. One of us went to school.” At the Saab she lays the sign face-down on the back seat beside the board, gently, like it might wake up.

response: He doesn’t say anything. He kisses her again, the sign still in her hand against his neck.
The man in the vest says “Ma’am” a second time, and gives up.

s11a.slug: SATURDAY · 8:05 PM · THE SAAB, THE 101 NORTH
body: At the on-ramp she reaches over and turns it up — “For my cousin from Ohio” — and puts her foot down, and the Saab, nineteen years old and an orphan, goes up onto the 101 like it has a call time. The top’s up. The nose of the board rides between their headrests and smells of wax.

For the first ten miles he can’t look at her. He looks at the road, the dash, the eyeliner sign face-down on the back seat, his own hands. She can’t stop smiling at the road. Every exit sign gets it. A Ralphs truck gets it.
“Hi,” she says finally, with her eyes on the lane, in a voice for a party where nobody knows anybody. “I’m the girl from the phone.”
“We’ve met.”
“We’ve *spoken*.”
She lets that ride for a whole exit, and doesn’t look over to check. His ears are hot to the tips. She drums the wheel in time with the song and lets him burn.
“My father says to tell you the Browns won four straight,” he says. “He said you’d want to know.”

Skye takes a hand off the wheel and puts it over her heart. “Tell Frank Costigan I’m *overcome*.” A lane change, no signal. “What’s a Brown? Is it a bird? Tell him I said that. No — tell him I cried.”

Past Goleta she brings the music down with one finger. “So. Tomorrow.” She gives it to him fast, like a call sheet: two-forty, West Hollywood, a back room behind a hedge, her mother, Corinne, a valet. And then she stops doing it fast. “I’m more nervous than I’m letting on,” she says. “And I’m letting on.”
The road comes down to the water. West of town the lights quit, and the coast goes black on the left, and out on the black the platforms sit lit up a long way offshore, little and gold and patient.

“Tomorrow matters,” Skye says. “I don’t want tonight to be the thing I’m thinking about at lunch.” She glances at him and back at the road. “So Ted gets you. That’s why. Not because I don’t want you. Because I do, and tomorrow at two-forty I have to sit across a table from my mother and not have it on my face.”

choices.text: *Open the ones you saved. Now, with her watching.*
response: He takes the RAZR out of his jacket. She sees what he’s doing and doesn’t say a word about it. At Refugio she puts the blinker on for the empty road, pulls onto the shoulder, sets the brake, and reaches up and clicks on the dome light. She turns in her seat with her knees up and her back against the door, and watches him. Not the screen. His face.

response.text: The window, stamp-sized and grainy under the dome light — two of her until he tilts it, and then one: her own reflection in her black glass at Del Playa, chin up, the surf breaking white straight through her.

response: He looks at it a long time.
When he looks up, she’s still looking at him, the dome light on her hair and the flannel open. “There he is,” Skye says, low.
She turns the light off, and pulls back out onto the 101 with the window cracked.

At two minutes to nine she pulls in at the corner of Mission, under a jacaranda with nothing on it, a block short of where anybody in a window could see. “Ted will be in a window with binoculars,” she says. “I know Ted.” She puts the Saab in neutral and turns to him with her back against her door.
“Ted has you at nine,” Skye says. “I have you at a quarter to twelve tomorrow. In between, you sleep in your dorm like a monk.”

She leans across him and opens his door, and kisses him once on the way back, and he’s on the sidewalk with the duffel while the Saab goes up Mission with its surfboard and one taillight brighter than the other.
