body: The Anchor at nine on a Saturday is the only lit window on the harbor side of Mission, a tank of yellow light with the sea lions hollering at it from the floats. Jack walks the last block from the corner with the duffel on his shoulder and his face put in order, and loses the order at the door, where the bell goes and the back booth turns around.

All four of them, and in the order he’d have bet. Laney is kneeling on the vinyl with a coffee spoon for a microphone. Margot sits upright against the window in a black turtleneck, Kevin beside her in a quarter-zip with his hands folded on the Formica, and in the corner, indoors, with the heat on, Theo, in the orange Browns hat and the brown-and-orange scarf Ma knitted in front of the news.
“Ladies and gentlemen,” Laney says into the spoon, “from Youngstown, Ohio: his platform is world peace and the Cleveland Browns, in that order, though he has been wrong before—”
“Sit,” Margot says. “She has been doing this since eight-thirty.”
“I *rehearsed*,” Laney says.
He sits on the outside, next to Theo, with the duffel between his feet. Propped against the sugar dispenser like a place card is an index card in purple Sharpie.

body.title: An index card, propped against the sugar
body.text: WELCOME BACK. 1. PIE. 2. NO QUESTIONS. 3. SEE ITEM 2.

body: “Item three refers the reader to item two,” Margot says. “Item two forbids the reader to ask why. The document is a closed loop.”
“It’s a *formatting choice*,” Laney says.

It is Laney being Laney: a welcome home with an agenda and a pie. Jack laughs, and keeps laughing a little past the joke, and Theo, who has not laughed, watches him do it with his chin in the scarf, as at a fever breaking.
Theo has already paid. A fifty sticks out from under the napkin dispenser, and nobody has ordered.
“You haven’t ordered,” Margot says.
“It’s called faith, Lindqvist,” Theo says. “Look it up.”
“I did. It isn’t that.”
“Theodore,” Laney tells the table, “has not taken that hat off since Christmas. He *slept* in it.”
“It’s a family heirloom,” Theo says.

He was in the middle of Youngstown when Jack came in, and he goes on with it: the eel, fried in rounds in a Pyrex at Frank’s elbow, which is a penance, for the men; Rosie, who has the Latin now, *Callinectes sapidus*, beautiful swimmer, savory, and says it at the table like a grace; Gina and the Flip camera; the stocking with his name on it in glitter glue, still wet on Christmas morning.
“Theodore cried at a stocking,” Laney says.
“Glitter is an irritant.”
He gets every detail right and tells it better than it happened, and Jack lets him have all of it and doesn’t add a word.
“Contestant Lindqvist,” Laney says, and points the spoon. “Portland.”
“Instructive.”
“That means awful.”

“It means my mother and her colleagues spent Christmas Eve arguing over whether Christmas is derivative of the Saturnalia, and I was asked to adjudicate. I said it was a category error. No one spoke to me until the pie.”
“Fourteen relatives, fourteen knees,” Kevin says, to nobody in particular. “My mother tells everyone I’m already a doctor, so they’ve started paying in rice cookers.”
“Mine was Dallas,” Laney says. “Mama cried at the fireworks *before* the fireworks. We have it on tape.”
Kevin has been studying Jack’s face with his head tilted. “Respectfully,” he says, “you look rested.”
“I was in Ohio.”
“I know. That’s the finding.”
“You’ve acquired a glow,” Margot says. “In Ohio. In January. That’s a statistical anomaly.”
“Lentils. Two spoons. I’m told I’ll be rich by Easter.”
“That is a folk belief in legume form,” Margot says.

Gloria arrives at the end of the booth with one plate, no pad, no check: a wedge of boysenberry with its insides running purple onto the china. She sets it in front of Jack and a fork beside it, says, “Tuesday. Seven,” and goes. Through the pass-through the kitchen radio is playing the song that has been on every radio in America since the fall, and Rudy, at the grill with his back to the booth, raises a spatula in Jack’s direction without turning around and says “Mijo,” softly, and not a decibel more.
Theo looks at the pie. Then at Jack. Then he takes a long drink of water.
“Since when,” Laney says, “do you eat boysenberry?”
“That was a question,” Margot says.
“That was an observation with a question mark on it.”
“Since Gloria put it in front of me,” Jack says, and picks up the fork.
“Okay. Business.” Laney taps the spoon on the card. “Tomorrow at four I’m getting Lena. Kevin’s driving. Her grandmother sent a king cake, and she is carrying it through two airports on her *lap*.”
“I know,” Jack says.
Laney looks at him over her Dr Pepper and takes her time with the straw. Then the spoon is a microphone again.
“So, fireman. Who picked you up?”
“Item two,” Margot says.
“It’s not a question. It’s a *logistics inquiry*.”
Theo studies a menu he has known by heart since August.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band.

body: At twenty past five that morning Theo came into 412 in the orange hat with sand on his shoes, and sat on his bed in the dark to take them off, and Jack heard all of it and lay still. At the nine-thirty at St. Brendan’s it was the Baptism of the Lord, the Christmas season going out in white — Osei at the altar in the white vestments, the heavens opened in Luke, *You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased* — and at twenty to twelve the Saab was at the Delgado curb, five minutes early, top down, her bare feet up on the dash. Rincon. Ventura. They didn’t say a word for forty miles, which for her is a medical event; and then on the 405 she said all of it at once — the hedge, the valet, which fork, her mother’s laugh and her mother’s other laugh — with her hand on the gearshift and his over it.

The restaurant is behind a hedge you could lose a car in. There’s a valet in a vest, and across the street a man leaning on a fence with a camera on a strap and nothing else to do, and Corinne has arranged — Skye tells him this in the alley — for the two of them to come in through the kitchen, past a man scaling fish who doesn’t look up. The back room has a skylight, four tables, and one of them set. At it: two women, a legal pad, a BlackBerry, a manila folder squared to the edge of the cloth, and a basket of bread. He doesn’t look at the bread.

Debbie Callender gets up. She is thirty-nine on paper, small and gold and finished, in cream, with Skye’s mouth and none of Skye’s freckles, and a voice with carpet in it. “Jack. *Jack.* Sit, sit, sit.”
He very nearly laughs. Across the table Skye looks hard at her water.

Debbie looks him over, top to bottom and back up: the blazer from the rain; the Goodwill tag still on the inside of the cuff, which she finds in about a second and a half; the St. Michael at his open collar, which she touches, briefly, with one fingernail. “Oh, he’s *Catholic*,” she tells Corinne, the way you’d say *Capricorn*.

Corinne Waxman doesn’t get up. She’s younger than Debbie and dressed like a fountain pen, all black and one gold clip, and she reads her BlackBerry the way other people read the room. Beverly Hills, Skye said in the alley — the kind of firm that answers its phone with its own name and nothing else. “Corinne,” Corinne says, by way of hello, and shakes his hand with the other one still scrolling. The folder stays shut by her plate.

Skye is in a green dress her mother picked, with sleeves, and her hair is up the way somebody else put it up, and before the bread has gone around once her shoes are off under the table. While Corinne is reading something she leans to him, very low. “Watch. She’s going to ask what your father does in the form of a question about your shoes.”
“Those are nice shoes,” Debbie says, to his feet. “What are those?”
“Florsheims. They’re my father’s.”
“And what does he do, your father?”
Under the table Skye’s bare foot taps his once: *told you*.
“GM,” Jack says. “Lordstown. The plant.”
“*GM!*” Debbie’s hand comes down on his sleeve. “I did a Chevy spot in ’94. A Lumina. I was the mom who forgets the lunch.”
Into her water glass, in a clipped murmur that belongs to the woman across from her, Skye says, “*Heartland. We love a heartland.*”
His father put twenty-six years into the line at Lordstown and has been on a list at the union hall since June. “That was a good car,” Jack says. It was not.
“And you’re studying —”
“Philosophy.”
Corinne looks up from the BlackBerry for the first time. “Is that employable?”
“No.”
She types something with her thumb.
“Skye was the little girl in the burger spot,” Debbie tells him, warming. “‘*Is that a* pickle?’ People still say it to her in —”
“Mother.”
“Baby, it’s a *compliment*.”

“I Googled you,” Corinne says. She scrolls. “There are a lot of Jack Costigans. Most of them are dead. You’re the one with a *Vindicator* box score — twelve points, no picture, thank God. Your name on a volunteer list for an Advent party at a Newman Center. Your Facebook, which is boring, which I love. One mutual friend with Skye.” She looks at him over the top of the BlackBerry. “And Skye tells me you room with Richard Vance’s son.”
“*Teddy!*” Debbie says. “Is he *eating*?”
“He’s eating.”
“He was the skinniest thing on that lot. Tell him Debbie says eat.”
“Which brings us,” Corinne says, “to this.” She turns the BlackBerry around on the cloth and slides it to him with one finger.

It’s a blog — the kind Corinne reads before the trades, pink and black, a banner of other people’s faces — and under the banner, the size of a stamp, a still from a video: a rope, a tile floor, the back of a Carhartt, a girl on her toes in sunglasses pushed up into her hair with both hands in the back of somebody’s head. You can’t see his face. You can see hers.

The airport comes down off Skye’s page today; the blogs she can live with — a blurry girl and the back of a coat is a rumor, and rumors are free. No photographs of the two of them, anywhere, by anybody, unless she has seen it first. If anyone asks — a waiter, a cousin, his mother — he is *a friend from school*. Through the glass he can see the two of them out among the potted lemons: Corinne holding the BlackBerry up between them, and Skye talking — fast, both hands, her shoulders up around her ears — in a way he hasn’t seen her talk to anybody. s15.music: Florence + the Machine — “Dog Days Are Over”
body: Out of the city she doesn’t talk, and he lets her not. It’s dark by Ventura. At Carpinteria she sits up behind the wheel and does Corinne saying *managed first sighting* — as a weather girl, as a eulogy, as an airline captain on descent, as a fortune-teller reading it off her own palm, as Corinne in labor, nine ways in all, the ninth in a whisper — and he laughs until he has his forehead against the window. The Marisol exit comes up green in the headlights and goes by.
“Not yet,” Skye says.

Buellton is a strip of light at the bottom of the dark: motels, a steakhouse sign, a feed store shut for the night. She takes the exit like she lives there and pulls in under the canopy of a gas station that isn’t anybody’s in particular, island four, and turns off the engine, and sits with both hands on the wheel.
“This is where you pushed,” she says.

She leaves the doors open and the radio going, and the song goes out over the empty islands. She gets out barefoot onto the concrete and works the pump herself, and hands him the squeegee because he’s standing there, and he does the windshield, bugs and salt and a thumbprint of eyeliner low in one corner of the glass. She leans on the fender with the nozzle ticking in the tank and takes out the white iPhone and frowns at it, thumbing, the same frown she gives a script.
“Come here,” she says. “No — closer. Face me. No. Face *it*.”

She turns the iPhone around so its one eye is on the two of them and holds it out at arm’s length over the pump, where neither of them can see a thing on the screen. “There’s no way to aim,” she says. “That’s the point.” One: the shutter noise, fake and cheerful. Two. On the third she turns her head and puts her mouth on the corner of his, and he laughs into it.

She brings the phone in and looks under the canopy light. The first is two foreheads and a price sign. The second is his eyes shut. The third is her mouth on his face and his face doing what it does, and the gas station going white behind them like a stage. “That one.”

“Corinne said take it down,” she says, thumbing, “so I took it down. In the car, on Sunset, with her on speaker listening to me do it.” Her thumb stops over the screen. “She didn’t say a word about putting one up.”

He still has the squeegee. On the little screen, over her arm, it’s Facebook — her own face at the top, small — and under it *Relationship Status*, and she has already chosen *In a Relationship*, and there’s a box after it that says *with*. Her thumb goes into the box. J-a-c-k, space, C-o-s — and his own face comes up out of her phone, the profile picture, looking surprised to be there, waiting to be picked.
“Corinne’s going to —” he says.
“Corinne’s going to call me in about forty minutes.” She doesn’t look up. “I’d like to be in the bath.”
She presses it.

The phone tells her it’s waiting on him. She reads that and bites the inside of her cheek, and taps through something he can’t follow, and her face goes off the top of the screen and a blank blue page comes up asking who’s there. She holds it out to him across the pump.
“Your turn.”

He has never held a phone with no keys. He types his own email address with one finger, hunting, backing up over the wrong letters, while she turns politely away and studies the price of diesel; then his password, the same way. And it’s there when the page comes up, the first thing, waiting:

body: “You told Danny before me,” Ma says. “You’re telling me before the computer. I’ll take it.”
And under that, lower, with the dish towel somewhere in it: “Thank you for calling me first.”
“Yeah, Ma.”

Back under the canopy the Saab’s doors are still open and the song is still going out over the concrete. Skye is sitting sideways in the driver’s seat with her bare feet on the ground, looking at the road, not at him. At the next island a pickup rolls over the hose, and the bell goes.

“You were on that phone with Lena all break,” Ma says. “Two hours on my kitchen floor with my cord through the pantry door, and then every single night — the garage, the porch, my eggs sitting an hour in the truck in the Giant Eagle lot.”
He looks at the air hose coiled on its hook.
“She’s still got a boyfriend, Ma,” he says. “He wrote a song for her. It was good.”
Ma doesn’t say anything.

In Youngstown the refrigerator runs. In Buellton the wind gets in under the edge of the canopy and turns a paper cup over and over across the lot. He can tell she wants to say something. She takes a breath for it and doesn’t use it, and takes another, and he stands at the air pump with the RAZR hot against his ear and Skye’s phone asleep in his other hand, and waits for her to find the way in, and she doesn’t find it; and he can’t find what it would be, either — what she’d say, or what he’d say back if she did. The bell at the next island goes again.
“Okay,” Ma says.
“Okay.”
Neither one of them is the thing. Then she’s gone, and it’s the wind.

He walks back across the lot under the canopy lights with both phones. Skye watches him come and doesn’t get up. He wakes her phone with his thumb and the request is still there where he left it, and he presses Confirm. She watches his thumb, not the screen.

The taquería is across the frontage road: a counter, four stools, a hand-lettered menu, a man in a paper hat. They eat standing up, al pastor off paper plates, and she eats in front of him — three tacos, both hands, lime running down her wrist, talking with her mouth full about the man in the paper hat’s life, which she has worked out entirely: a daughter at Cal Poly, a bad knee, a wife who does the books and the lettering on the menu, and he hasn’t been to the beach since 1986, which is twenty minutes from here, which is a crime. Her iPhone lies face-down on the counter by the hot sauce and buzzes against the Formica. “That’s my mother.” It stops; it starts. “That’s Corinne.” It stops; it starts. “That’s my mother again.” She doesn’t turn it over. She asks the man for another lime.

At eight fifty-two she stops at the Delgado curb with the engine running and the top up against the damp. Behind him the dorm is lit window over window, everybody back. She leans to look past him at all of it, and then at him.
“Tomorrow everybody finds out what I already knew,” Skye says.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything.

body: Priya’s laminated sign is back on the fourth-floor stairwell door: WELCOME BACK. QUIET HOURS RESUME AT 10 P.M., SUNDAY–THURSDAY. THIS MEANS YOU. —P.R. From behind the door of 420 comes Doug’s voice, patient, to a stranger on a headset: “Dude. No. *Behind* it.” The strap of the duffel is cutting into Jack’s shoulder. He is still smiling a little, at nothing, in a hallway, and he lets the strap dig.

The door of 412 opens before he gets to it. Laney comes out with her laptop shut under one arm and her phone in the other fist, in the Pi Lam hoodie, no lipstick, her mouth a straight line. She sees him. For the first time since August she looks at him and says nothing, not *fireman*, not his name, and goes by with her shoulder a few inches from his duffel and down the hall to the east stairwell, and the fire door shuts on the sound of her feet.
“Laney?” he says, to the door.
Jack looks after her. Then he goes in.

412 has one lamp lit and the window open a crack, and the room smells of kelp and, faintly, of somebody’s vanilla. Theo is on his bed in his socks with his eyes on the ceiling and the orange hat hanging from the bedpost by its brim. The iPhone on his chest is face-up, and it buzzes and lights the underside of his chin. He looks at it, and turns it face-down.
“Hey,” Jack says.
“Congratulations, Costigan.” To the ceiling. No *Father Jack*, no *my moral compass*: just the surname, laid down flat.
“Thanks.” Jack lets the duffel off his shoulder onto his bed.
“Callender changed it herself,” Theo says.
It takes Jack a second. “How do you know?”
“Because Corinne would have made it a premiere.”
Theo turns his head on the pillow, looks at him, and looks back up. Jack sits down on his own bed with his shoes still on.
“Go to sleep,” Theo says. He reaches over his head and the lamp goes out. In the dark: “Monday is going to be a long day.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. body: The twelve-ten on the first Monday back is thin and a little dazed, and Fr. Osei has the green on, the first green since November. The Gospel is Mark, the first chapter, the shore: *Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.* Simon and Andrew abandon their nets on the spot, and the next two are called while they are mending theirs. “Ordinary Time,” Osei says in a homily of ninety seconds, “is when He asks. Nothing is happening. This is why He picks it.”
Third pew on the Gospel side, where Lena has knelt at nearly every twelve-ten since September, a freshman sits with his backpack on the kneeler.

At the sign of peace Becca, across the aisle, turns around and holds out her hand, and he takes it. “Peace be with you.” “And also with you.” Her hand is dry and brief, and she is facing the altar again before his has let go.

body.text: Jack goes up with the line and receives, and comes back down the side aisle with his hands folded and his eyes on the tile.
body.else: When the line forms Jack stays where he is, with his hands on the back of the pew in front of him, and makes a spiritual communion, the old prayer, to the sound of other people’s shoes.

body: Afterward the line out the door is a Monday line: Mrs. Fitch with the announcements and a lanyard, Joey Abruzzo telling a freshman, at the volume of a kickoff, that the twelve-ten is the best-kept secret on campus, and under the bell Osei, in the green, with his glasses on their cord, saying *Akwaaba, akwaaba* to everyone who has been away. When it is Jack’s turn Osei takes his hand in both of his own and holds him at arm’s length.
“Let me look at you.” It is a physician’s look and it lasts one second. “You have your color. In December I was prepared to prescribe sleep.”
“I slept.”
“So I see.” He lets go of the hand. “Well?”
“Father. The errand.”
“Ah. And?”
“Father Dom says we’ll see.”
The laugh starts somewhere near the belt and keeps climbing, and heads turn the length of the steps. “Then we will,” Osei says, and wipes an eye with the back of his wrist.

body.text: “I went at home, Father,” Jack says. “Saturday before last.”
“Good,” Osei says. “Welcome back.”
“Saturday, Father?” Jack says.
“Three-thirty,” Osei says. “I’ll leave the light on.”
“Welcome back, Jack,” Osei says. And Jack doesn’t ask about Saturday.

body: At the bottom of the steps someone has been waiting her turn, and now she isn’t: Becca, with her grandmother’s rosary wound twice around her wrist and her braid over one shoulder and the clipboard against her chest, coming up toward him with her face already open. Jack is on the third step from the top. He stays on it. The strap of his bag is in his fist.

“I saw,” Becca says. She stops one step below him, so that their eyes are level. “Last night, on the News Feed. I made myself wait until after Mass to decide how I felt, because I didn’t want to decide it in the middle of the Creed. And I decided. She’s so pretty, Jack. And she looks — she looks really happy. I’m really happy for you.”

“I prayed for you over Christmas,” she says. “That you’d be happy. So.” She laughs at herself, short, and pushes the braid back. “I also did a Glory Be for both of you at breakfast. Twice. It’s short. And I’m good, by the way, in case you were going to wonder. I have a hermit crab and a lab section.”
“And Thomas saw snow,” she says. “In Coeur d’Alene. He did not care for it.” She taps the clipboard. “Coffee and Donuts is still Sundays. The maple bars are yours. I told Mrs. Fitch.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home.

Hollis 302 is the room it was in the fall — the long table, the radiator, the window over the eucalyptus — with the spring’s twelve around it. Caleb has the chair nearest the head of the table and a new pad of Post-its squared in front of him. Evan Marsh, Hale’s reader again this term, comes around the table laying a syllabus at every place without looking at anyone. Jack takes the chair at the end by the door, under the clock, and puts his bag on the floor against his leg. By five to one every chair at the window end is taken.
Yusuf drops into the chair beside Jack’s with a coffee. “Good Christmas?”
“Good. Yours?”

“My brother’s home.” He takes the lid off the coffee and blows across it. “My father’s line has eleven weeks. He’s been bringing his tools home one at a time so my mother won’t notice. She’s cleared a shelf.”

Hale comes in at six past one with wine on his cuff from some earlier year and no dog, and a step behind him, as if she timed it to the second, Lena — a white bakery box in both hands, a new cardigan, gray, buttoned to the throat, her hair up off her neck with a pencil through it. It’s the first time he has seen her since the checkpoint at the airport in December. She looks down the table for a chair, and there is one: the corner, beside his.
She sets the box in the middle of the table, with a card propped against it in her hand: FOR THE SEMINAR. Then she sits down next to him.
“Hi, Jack,” she says. “Happy New Year.”
It’s a voice for anybody. She moves her chair an inch so her elbow won’t touch his, and says “Sorry” for the inch, and opens her syllabus.
“Good afternoon, survivors.” Hale stops at the box. “What is this.”
“King cake, Professor,” Lena says. “It’s Carnival. There’s a baby in it somewhere, and whoever gets the baby buys the next one.”
Hale cuts the first slice himself, bites, and draws out from between his teeth a pink plastic baby. He holds it up to the window and turns it in the light. “I appear to have been chosen.”
“Then you buy the next one, Professor.”
The box goes down the table hand to hand. Jack takes a piece when it reaches him. Purple sugar and green and gold, on his fingers and on the syllabus.
“Last week I asked you for a novel that lied to you,” Hale says. “Go.”

Caleb says *Ender’s Game*: it told him being the smartest boy in the room was a moral position, and he was homeschooled, so he was the only boy in the room. Yusuf says *The Fountainhead*. “It told me architects were interesting.” Lena says *Gone with the Wind* — read at twelve in Mémère’s house in Breaux Bridge, and it told her the South was a lady somebody had done wrong. Jack says *On the Road*. It told him leaving and going somewhere are the same thing.
“Good,” Hale says. “Now. Can a made-up story tell the truth?”

Lena goes first, from the chair beside his, and she is brilliant. The book didn’t lie to her, she says. Mitchell did, and the book told on her. A novel is a confession nobody made — that’s why it can’t lie. It shows you exactly what somebody wanted, even when she meant to show you something else.

Jack takes the other side, which he has never taken at this table. Augustine wept for Dido, he says. Book One. He cried over a made-up woman on a made-up pyre and didn’t cry for himself, who was the one dying, and he called that the sickness. A made-up story can steal the tears you owe the truth. It’s a counterfeit, and a good one, and the good ones are the danger.

“That’s a good argument,” Lena tells the table, and takes it apart, courteously, one premise at a time: Augustine wrote thirteen books about himself so he could finally cry for the right person, and he learned the shape of it from Virgil, and he quoted Virgil the rest of his life — read the *City of God*; he never put him down. “But he’s right that it’s dangerous,” she says, and turns her pen end over end. “So is a knife.”
Hale turns his head down the table. “Mr. Costigan.”
“A knife doesn’t ask you to love it,” Jack says.

“That’s fair,” Lena says. “That’s a fair point.” She writes it in her margin. Then she doesn’t put the pen down. “Though since we’re in the *Aeneid*. Book Four. Everybody cries for Dido. Nobody asks how she got up on the pyre.”
“Aeneas left.”

“Aeneas let her think it was one thing all winter,” Lena says, pleasantly, to Hale, “and then he got his orders from a god nobody else heard, and went down to the ships in the dark. Virgil gives him a speech. It’s a very good speech. He’d had a while to work on it.”
“He never called it a marriage,” Jack says. “He says so. To her face.”
“He didn’t have to call it anything. He stayed all winter.” She turns a page she isn’t reading. “It’s a very convenient god.”
“She knew who he was from the first night. She knew he had somewhere to be.”
“She knew what he told her.”

Across the table Yusuf has stopped blowing on his coffee. Caleb has stopped writing. Her shoulder is an inch from his and has been since six past one, and neither of them has looked at the other once.

Hale caps his pen. “Miss Broussard. For the better part of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it.” He looks from her to Jack and back. “I find I care for this even less. Carthage is not on the syllabus. Kindly leave it there.”
“Yes, Professor,” Lena says. “Happy New Year, Professor.”
She has been polite to him for an hour, every minute of it but ten. She has never been polite to him in her life.
The chairs go back. Lena’s tin is in the front pocket of his bag, where it rode back from Ohio, and he doesn’t take it out.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday nobody saw her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for most of an hour. Then Dido.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the better part of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus.

response: He catches her at the door. “Happy New Year, Lena. For real.”
“You too, Jack.” The one o’clock voice again, as if the last ten minutes happened to somebody else. She goes past him into the hall with her bag on her shoulder.

choices.text: “You owe me a piece of king cake.”
response: He catches her at the door. “You owe me a piece of king cake.”
She looks back at the box on the table, where two pieces are going stale under their sugar.
“It’s on the table, Jack. Same as everybody’s.”
She goes.

He stays at his end of the table and puts the syllabus in his bag. Hale’s plastic baby is standing up on the wood where Hale left it, facing the window. She goes down the stairs with Laney’s scarf around her neck and the empty box under her arm.

s18a.slug: MONDAY · 2:25 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE BACK STEPS
body: The back steps of Hollis come down onto the service lot: a dumpster, a Facilities cart, a TA’s bike chained to the rail without its front wheel, and the eucalyptus over all of it, dropping bark on the asphalt in long curls. Jack sits on the third step with the bag between his feet. It is the first time today he has been by himself.

Behind him the fire door bangs open and two girls come out with their own cigarettes, see him, and take them down to the far end of the lot by the dumpster. Up the hill somebody with a window open is learning the trumpet one note at a time.

In the front pocket of the bag, the tin. Eleven, her count. In the side pocket, his own pack, which rode to Ohio and back at the bottom of the duffel under everything. His thumb finds the lighter in his coat pocket and rests on the wheel.

response: He takes one out of his own pack and lights it with his back to the wind. The smoke goes up into the eucalyptus and comes apart there.
He smokes it down on the steps with the bag between his feet, and it doesn’t help, and he didn’t think it would.

choices.text: *Put the pack back in the bag.*
response: He puts the pack back where it was, under the syllabus. Down by the dumpster the two girls finish theirs and come back up past him and go in. The zipper; the eucalyptus; a bell somewhere for the two-thirty.
He opens the tin on his knee and counts them with one finger. The filters tick against the lid.
Eleven.
He shuts it and puts it back in the front pocket, and zips the pocket, and sits a little longer with his hand on the bag.

s19.slug: MONDAY · 8:00 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: At five to eight, before Theo gets to the remote, the TV in the Fishbowl is on ESPN, and ESPN has Mark McGwire: a still of him in a Cardinals cap, a graphic, and an anchor reading off a card what he put out that afternoon. *I wish I had never touched steroids. It was foolish and it was a mistake.* At eight Theo takes the remote off the top of the set, where Doug left it, and puts on ABC without asking anybody. On a Monday night in the Fishbowl it was never a question.

The Fishbowl is the lounge off the Delgado lobby, glass on two sides, so the lobby can see in and everybody inside has agreed to forget it: three couches that have seen things, a coffee table ringed by a semester of cans, a foosball table that lost a goalie in October and has played a man short ever since. Margot is in the armchair with her Docs up on the coffee table and a notebook open on her knee. Kevin has an orgo text in his lap, open to a page he hasn’t turned since the opening credits. Doug Pruitt is on the carpet with his back against the couch, in a shirt with a Tauren on it, eating Froot Loops dry out of the box.
The far end of the middle couch, where Laney sits every week and narrates the rose ceremony for the room, is empty.

“Laney’s in 217 tonight,” Theo says, politely, when he sees Jack look at it. That’s all. He settles into his own end with his ankles crossed and the orange hat on the arm beside him, and gives the television his attention.

Skye has the arm of the couch at Jack’s end. She came in barefoot with her flats in her hand and a man’s flannel over a tank top, the cuffs rolled four times, and she sits up on the arm with her feet on the cushion beside his thigh and one hand resting at the back of his neck, not doing anything with it, just there, warm. She looks the Fishbowl over from the arm of the couch — the doors, the glass, who’s sitting where — and Jack watches her learn it.
“I’ve played three dormitories,” she says. “I’ve never been in one.”

At two minutes past eight Priya comes across the lobby with a clipboard against her chest — the spring floor sign-up, color-coded tabs — and stops in the Fishbowl doorway, because there is a person in it she has not cleared.
“Name?”
“Skye.”
“Last name?”
“Callender.”
Priya writes it down without a flicker. She doesn’t own a television; she has said so, at a floor meeting, as a policy. “Guest of?”
“Four-twelve,” Jack says.

body.title: 4th floor guest log
body.text: 8:02 p.m. · Callender, S. · guest of 412

body: “Quiet hours start at ten. I’m going to need you to know that.” And Priya goes back out across the lobby with the clipboard, and Skye turns to Jack with both hands over her heart and mouths, enormous, *She has no idea who I am.*
Theo, from his end, without moving anything but his eyes: “Callender.”
“Ted.”
Margot writes *TED* in her notebook, and underlines it.
Kevin is already on his feet with his hand out — the quarter-zip, the big smile, a welcome-table grip. “Kevin. Four-twenty. Hi. Welcome to the Fishbowl.”
“It’s glass,” Margot says.
“That’s the whole joke,” Kevin says. “We’re not a creative floor.”
From the floor Doug lifts the Froot Loops in salute. “Doug. Dude. My mom watches your —”

“Everybody’s mom,” Skye says, kindly. She sits back on the arm of the couch and casts the room, because she can’t not. She points with her chin. “That end of the couch is Ted’s. He’s the only one who sits there, and he’s holding the remote because it’s a show he hates.”
“Correct,” Margot says. “He times the ceremony with a stopwatch.”
“You,” to Kevin, “organize things. You know everybody’s birthday.”
Kevin laughs. “Guilty.”
“And you two,” Skye says, to Margot and to Doug on the carpet at Margot’s feet, “are sleeping together, and you think it’s a secret.”
Doug looks into the cereal box.
“Fascinating,” Margot says. “Wrong. But fascinating.”
“Dude,” Doug says. “She doesn’t even *sleep*.”
“Then I’m recasting,” says Skye, and takes her hand off Jack’s neck long enough to shake Doug’s, cereal dust and all.

By the rose ceremony the candles are lit on the TV and the women are standing on risers in gowns, and a man with a silver tray of roses is waiting at the side of the set, and the host comes out to say it’s the final rose tonight as if it has never happened before. A woman is called down. *Will you accept this rose?*

“Watch her,” Skye says. “Everything on that show is written except the yes. And the yes is the most produced word on television. She’s been standing on that mark since four in the afternoon. Somebody told her where her light is. Somebody’s going to tell her after, the boom dipped, do it again.” The woman on the screen says yes. Skye says it with her, a hair ahead, exactly the same: *Yes.*
Doug stops eating.

“And your baseball player.” She sits up straighter on the arm of the couch, and her thumb starts going on an invisible BlackBerry, and the woman across the table at lunch is suddenly in the Fishbowl in the flesh. “*I wish I had never touched steroids. It was foolish and it was a mistake.*” And she’s herself again. “That’s Corinne. That’s a publicist. People who are sorry don’t say *it was foolish and it was a mistake*. They say *I’m sorry*, and then they look at the floor. That’s two sentences in one coat so it’ll sound like it cost him something. You can hear the meeting.”
“So somebody wrote it,” Jack says. “So what. It can still be true when he says it.”
“Can it?”

“I say a sentence every time I go in the box that somebody wrote before my grandmother was born. *O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee.* I didn’t write it. I’m not any less sorry. The Creed’s sixteen hundred years old — the people at the nine-thirty didn’t make it up on the way in. People get married in words a bishop picked out in a room. They’re not lying.” He leans forward with his elbows on his knees. “They’re truest when you say them like they’re yours. That’s what they’re for. You grow into them.”
The Fishbowl has turned from the TV to the couch. It knows how to watch an argument; it’s had practice.

Skye reaches down beside the couch into her canvas bag and comes up with a paperback — a used one, the spine already broken by somebody else, a Coffee Bean receipt sticking out of it for a bookmark. *Orthodoxy*. She doesn’t have to hunt for the page.

“Your G. K. says tradition is votes for the dead. Here: *It is the democracy of the dead.*” She shuts it on her finger. “Fine. The dead get a vote. I’m very pro-dead. But they don’t get to say it *for* you. You still have to mean it. And nobody out here can check.”
“You don’t check from out there,” Jack says. “You watch what the man does next.”
“That’s my whole job.” She points the book at the TV, where there’s only a man with a tray left to point at. “What he does next is the only part nobody can write.”

Somewhere in the last minute Kevin has closed the orgo book on his finger. Now he stands up with it under his arm. “Anybody want anything? I’m going down to the machines.” No takers. He goes out through the glass and across the lobby to the basement stairs.

Margot puts her pen down. “Goffman,” she says. “*The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life*. 1956. Everyone’s performing. The only question is which audience.” She looks at Skye straight on. “That was the better argument. I find that annoying. I’d like to interview you sometime. For research.”
“I’d love that,” Skye says. “Bring Costigan. He can watch me win.”
Theo isn’t watching the TV. Theo is watching Jack.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it.

response: “Then nothing’s true till somebody watches the next part.”

“Yes.” She’s off the arm of the couch and down onto the cushion beside him, knees up, facing him, delighted, the book still on her finger. “Yes. Welcome to my industry. Come in, wipe your feet, nothing’s true till the second season.” She taps the paperback once against his chest. “Do that again. Push me like that again.”
In the quiet after it, from the floor, with his mouth full of Froot Loops, Doug Pruitt says, happily, to the room: “Dude. This is like when you and Lena do it.”
Nobody says anything. Theo looks at the TV. Margot looks at her notebook.
Skye reaches over and picks a thread off Jack’s sleeve, at the cuff, and drops it on the carpet. Jack’s hands are on his knees, and he leaves them there.
On the screen a woman without a rose is being walked out to a car. Kevin comes back up from the basement with a Snapple he doesn’t open.

s20.slug: MONDAY · 10:40 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM

body.text: He knows the window first. Before the lamp, before the bed, before her, the black glass over the mattress, and the white line of the surf low across it.

body: The heater is still broken. There are three blankets on the mattress under the window, and on top of them, since she took it off him in the doorway and threw it there, his Carhartt, for a fourth. The working half of the Christmas lights is still working. Under the porch, Tomás’s boards lean where the boys won’t let them on the rack, and down the hall the darkroom door is shut on its red strip of light, and she is still not allowed through it. She tells him so again on the way past, like it’s a ghost story.

On the floor by the bed there’s a boombox with a cracked tape door, Sol’s, and Skye kneels and puts a CD in it out of a case with no art left on it, and the room fills with something slow and low and expensive. “My mother’s,” she says. “She played it in the car to every audition I ever had. I’d be in the back doing my sides, and she’d be up front doing this.” She sways once, on her knees, to show him. “I find it very relaxing. That’s a lie.”
Then she hands him a textbook.

*College Algebra*, the fifth edition, the price sticker from the campus store still on the spine. The letter came to her mother’s over the break, she tells him, and she’s been carrying it around in her bag ever since like a parking ticket she’s proud of; today was the first class. “Not remedial,” Skye says. “*College.*” She lies down on her stomach across the three blankets with her chin on her fists and her bare feet in the air. “Your pie got me out of remedial. I’m naming it.”
“You can’t name a pie.”
“I named a parrot’s therapist. Problem fourteen.”

Problem fourteen is a line through two points. He does it in her margin with her pencil, a little proudly, and she reads it, checks it against the back of the book, and pays for problem fifteen with a kiss, an advance against services; she says that’s standard. Fifteen costs two. By eighteen they’ve stopped keeping track of the rate.
Twenty-two is a word problem: a jacket marked down twenty percent, and then twenty percent off the sale price. What percent off the original? “Forty,” Jack says.

“Thirty-six.” She doesn’t even pick up the pencil. “It’s never forty. I’ve been marked down twice in my life, Jack. It’s thirty-six every time.” She checks the back of the book anyway, for show, and turns it around to him. Thirty-six.

His Greene is on the bed, where it fell out of his bag — *The End of the Affair*, Hale’s for the twenty-eighth. She picks it up and reads the back cover to herself, frowning at it, and he watches her get to the part about the vow.

“So she makes God a promise,” Skye says. “She doesn’t even believe in Him. She makes a promise to somebody she doesn’t think is there, and then she *keeps* it?” She turns it over to the cover. “That’s either the dumbest thing in this book or the only romantic thing in it.” She drops it off the end of the mattress, gently, onto the floor. “I’ll tell you which when you’ve read it. Do my homework.”
He doesn’t. She takes the textbook out of his hands and puts it on the floor with the Greene, and reaches past him and tilts the lampshade so the light comes down on the bed.
“One thing,” she says. “One thing you said to me on the phone. Here. With the lamp on, and your eyes open.”

She leaves the lamp on. “You wanted to see,” she says. So he looks at her, in the light, where he’s allowed to — her face first, for a long time, and then the rest of her, and back up to her face, and she lets him take as long as he likes about it.

They get to where they have been before, and they get there fast; they know the way now, and nothing on the road surprises either of them. His shirt is somewhere. His jeans are on the floor with *College Algebra*. Her hair is everywhere.

Then Skye gets up on her knees on the blankets in the lamplight, and looks at him, and with her own two hands, not hurrying, takes off the last thing she has on, and drops it over the edge of the mattress, and lets him look.

He has never seen all of her before. She is long and brown from the sun down to where a suit has kept her pale, and the paleness is a shock, pale as the inside of her wrist; freckles across her shoulders as well as her nose; the sharp hipbones of somebody who paddles out in January; her breasts small and roughened with gooseflesh in the unheated room; a white seam of old scar under one knee that he has never heard the story of; and at her ankle the braided anklet. She’s left that on. She isn’t posing. She is letting herself be looked at by one person, on purpose, with a lamp on, and he can see in her face that she’s decided it, and what it costs.
The last thing he has on stays on him. That’s where the line is now. She lays her palm on his stomach just above it, warm, and leaves it there.

He wants her so much it’s a sound in his ears, under the music. And none of it is new to him anymore. That’s what’s new. Every word of this has been in his mouth already, in the dark, and the yes is lying right there at the end of it, worn smooth, close enough to pick up.

She comes down over him and takes his face in both her hands, so his eyes have to stay open, and the lamp is on both of them, and he can see the word coming up in her before she’s even ready to let it out.

s20a.slug: TUESDAY · 1:30 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: The CD has stopped. Under three blankets and the Carhartt it’s warm, and everywhere else in the room it’s January, and the surf comes through the glass over their heads, breaking and pulling back. Her feet are cold on his shins. He thought she was asleep.
“Who’d you call at the pump?”
He’s quiet long enough that she props up on an elbow in the dark. She watched him walk away, clear across the lot to the air hose, with a phone in each hand.
“My mother.”
She lies back down and leaves the next part to the surf.
“Nobody’s ever called their mother about me,” Skye says. “People call their *agents* about me.” She finds his hand under the blankets. “What did she ask you?”
He tells her two of the three things his mother said.
That she wanted to know if Skye was still asking.
“Tell her I’m in the waiting room,” Skye says. “I brought a magazine.”
And that he told his brother before he told her, and she told him she’d take it, since he was telling her before the computer.
Skye likes that. He can feel her like it, the breath she lets out against his shoulder. “Your brother first. Good.” Her thumb goes over his knuckles. “He’s in the folder I didn’t open.”
The third he keeps.

She falls asleep after that, for real — he can tell from her hand, gone heavy on his chest, and from her breathing, long and slow and no longer keeping time with his. He lies on his back and starts the night prayer the way his grandmother taught it to him at the edge of a bed on Glenwood Avenue, her hand on his head, in her Italian: *Angelo di Dio, che sei il mio custode* — and somewhere after the first line he loses it, and can’t find the rest, and lies there with it unfinished.

Over them the window is black. The half of the Christmas lights that still works gives the room back to the glass, faint, and in it, if he turns his head on the pillow, the two of them are there under the blankets, laid over the dark, and through them the white line of the surf, breaking.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math.
